description: Monitor a pull request through review and CI. Use when the user asks to monitor, watch, or babysit a PR.

# Babysit PR

Many repos have AI review bots. They're helpful, even if they are not always
right.

## Waiting

Never write your own watcher, polling loop, or `sleep` loop. Use one watcher
per PR: `watch_pull_request` in T3 Code, `pr-wait` everywhere else. Never run
both on the same PR. Every watcher on a GitHub account shares one rate limit.

### In T3 Code: `watch_pull_request`

Handle the existing checks and comments first. Then call
`watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you with a message when
a check fails, the required checks pass, someone comments or reviews, or the
branch conflicts.

- **Only the thread that owns the PR watches it.** If you are a delegated
  child task (a reviewer, a Sol round, any `delegate_task` child), never call
  `watch_pull_request`. The parent owns the PR. Do not watch PRs you are not
  working on.
- **A wake is news, not a merge decision.** Check the merge gate yourself.
- **Unwatch when you hand off.** A watched thread stays in Working and out of
  the user's inbox. When you stop (ready, blocked, or asking the user a question),
  call `unwatch_pull_request` first. A merge or close ends the watch on its
  own.
- **"Stopped watching, could not read it"** usually means GitHub's rate limit
  is used up. Run `gh api rate_limit --jq .resources.graphql` before you
  watch again. If `remaining` is near 0, wait for `reset` with one background
  command, then watch again. Never watch again in a tight loop.

### Everywhere else: `pr-wait`

Wait with `scripts/pr-wait` from this skill's directory (use its absolute
path).

```bash
pr-wait <pr> [--repo owner/name] [--until ready|green|any-change]
```

It prints one line per real event. It exits 0 when the `--until` condition is
met or the PR merges, 1 when it needs you (a required check failed, conflicts,
unresolved threads, PR closed), and 2 on bad input.

- `ready` (default): required checks green, Greptile or Macroscope reviewed the
  head, and no unresolved threads. Use this to babysit.
- `green`: required checks only. Use it when the repo has no Greptile or
  Macroscope.
- `any-change`: exit on the first event.

In Claude Code, run it with the Monitor tool (`timeout_ms: 3600000`), so each
line wakes you. Without a monitor, run it as one long command. It ends on its
own.

Start it again after you push, after you handle an exit 1, and after a resume.
It remembers what it already reported, so nothing that arrived in between is
lost. If it says another pid already watches the PR, do not start a second one.
Kill the old one only if its events do not reach you.

With either watcher: when an event needs no action, end your turn without a
message. Never post or say "still waiting".

## GitHub rate limits

`gh pr create`, `gh pr view`, and `gh pr checks` use GraphQL. When GraphQL is
used up, the REST limit is separate and usually still has room. Use
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n>` to read a PR, and
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs` for checks.

## Reviews

Only act on checks and comments newer than the latest push. Verify every bot
finding against the source before changing code. Fix real findings and CI
failures, distinguish repository failures from infrastructure flakes, and reply
with a written reason when dismissing false positives.

If the repo has `.macroscope/check-run-agents/*.md`, read those rules before you
reply to a Macroscope finding. Its findings cite them.

CodeRabbit is advisory. Treat its findings like any other finding, but never
wait for it and never hold a merge for it.

If a review bot leaves feedback you believe is not worth addressing, reply with
a written reason and resolve the comment. Use the `leaving-pr-comments` skill
for every comment posted on the user's behalf.

Screenshots and videos help as well, when you have a way to upload them.

Keep the PR at the size the user's goal needs. Review loops tend to grow a
PR one cheap-looking fix at a time. Fix real bugs in the intended case.
Decline the rest with a written reason, and list them as follow-ups:
unneeded tests, guards for edge cases that do not matter, extra integration
or compatibility, and small performance costs. Prefer the fix that deletes or
narrows code.

## Base branch and merging

Keep an eye on changes to `main` and rebase when needed. `pr-wait` reports when
new base commits touch this PR's files, and when the PR becomes BEHIND or DIRTY.
`watch_pull_request` reports conflicts only, so check for BEHIND yourself
before you call the PR ready.
If an overlapping PR makes this one obsolete, stop monitoring, report it to the
user, and ask before closing the PR unless closure was explicitly authorized.

If nothing has changed, stay quiet rather than posting filler comments. Stop
when `pr-wait` exits 0, or in T3 Code when the merge gate passes on the latest
head. Merge only when the user explicitly requested it;
otherwise report that the PR is ready. Right before a merge, run `git fetch` and
check the PR again. Never merge when it is BEHIND or DIRTY, or when base commits
that landed after the last green run touch this PR's files. Rebase, push, and
wait for green again.

Prefix every agent-authored comment left on the user's behalf with this GitHub
note callout:

```md
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 **<model> responding on behalf of <user>**

Actual comment starts here.
```

user's name or GitHub login.

attachments, for secrets and private details.

Setext underline, heading, signature footer, or a second attribution.

bots or reviewers, and written explanations used before resolving or
dismissing feedback. Do not add it to PR descriptions, commit messages, or text
the user explicitly asked to post verbatim without attribution.

Write the comment itself in a direct style:

- Lead with the conclusion.
- Cite the relevant code, behavior, check, or reproduction.
- Keep it concise and avoid filler, canned thanks, or status narration.
- Distinguish verified facts from judgment.

Preview the final Markdown before posting so quoting and blank lines render as
shown. After posting, verify that GitHub returned the comment or review URL.
Resolve a review thread only after its response was posted successfully.

# Takeover

Take responsibility for finishing the original goal while preserving the
original contributors' credit. Do not defend an implementation just because
another agent already built it.

Read the source PR, branch, or thread, including review findings and the user's
later corrections. Resolve the handoff to the actual code and current head,
and account for uncommitted work. Treat the handoff as context, not proof.

For a replacement PR, import the original commits onto a new branch and add
your fixes separately. Honor an explicitly requested in-place or stacked
continuation instead. Do not overwrite unrelated work or change the original
PR without authorization.

Preserve Git authorship and existing co-author trailers. Credit the original
contributors in the PR description and link the original PR when there is one.
If the work will be squashed, preserve human author/co-author credit in the
merge commit too, using verified identities rather than guessed emails. Model
attribution is not a substitute for contributor credit.

Use `modernize` to update the continuation against its intended base and
current architecture. Rework what is necessary to finish the same goal, not
unrelated features. Simplify the implementation without dropping intended
behavior or surfaces. Recheck the source PR too: it may have improved while
you were working.

Independently verify the original failure and realistic workflows, following
repository guidance and permissions. Green mocked tests do not prove the user
experience works. State what remains unverified.

When the requested finish includes a PR, use `file-pr` to file or update it,
then `babysit-pr` rather than stopping at creation. Use `leaving-pr-comments`
for replies. Merge or close the original PR only when authorized.

Report what you inherited, what you changed, how you verified it, how credit
was preserved, and any remaining decision.

# Five-PR delivery stacks

The current user policy is to accumulate five dependent PRs before integrating the
batch into master. Keep each layer coherent and reviewable. Assemble five layers
before the final combined merge to master.

```text
master ← PR1 ← PR2 ← PR3 ← PR4 ← PR5
```

The bottom PR targets master. Each later PR targets the preceding layer's branch,
so its review shows that layer's change. Use `stack/<batch>-<layer>-<description>`
for batch branches, including the first layer when conserving previews. Preserve the
legacy recreation checkpoint unchanged.

While an earlier layer runs CI, build the next dependent layer when its scope is
clear. Up to five layers may be in flight together. Keep fixes on their owning
branch, propagate them through dependent layers, and validate each resulting head.
Do not open a sixth layer or fold a partial batch into master merely to avoid a wait.

For each finalized PR, create an isolated get-green agent to inspect current-head
Actions and reviews, repair concrete failures and escalate uncertain fundamental
changes to the parent. Pending, missing or failed Actions is not green, but an
intermediate wait does not block assembling the later layers. The merge gate is the
last PR's complete combined head, with a successful named `Rules, build and mock
browser` job and no actionable review findings. Never remove assertions or suites
merely to obtain green checks.

Once five layers exist, assemble all changes on the last PR's branch and target that
PR directly at master. A dependent top branch already contains its ancestors; verify
that ancestry and fold in any missing layer or repair. Validate the final combined
head once instead of waiting for a new CI pass after every intermediate fold. Require
its complete current-head Actions/review gate before the single master merge. Earlier
open layers can target master so their included commits are accounted for by that
combined merge. If master changes during the batch, integrate it and validate the
resulting tree before the final merge. Verify the fetched head and resulting tree;
do not infer completion from a queued operation.

Stacking alone does not suppress preview builds. `vercel.json` sets
`git.deploymentEnabled["stack/**"]` to false, using Vercel's supported minimatch branch
rules. Pushes to those batch branches therefore skip automatic Vercel deployments.
Unspecified branches retain their normal behavior, including master. Keeping every
layer under `stack/**` leaves the one master merge as the automatic production
deployment for a batch. A deliberate preview on another branch remains optional.

See [Vercel's Git configuration](https://vercel.com/docs/project-configuration/git-configuration).

rule enables it. A deliberate intermediate preview skip is expected; continue to
require Actions and reviews. Only the previously observed daily deployment-quota
failure is waived. Investigate other actual deployment failures, and do not retry
deployments or change billing as a response to quota exhaustion.

Validate repository configuration before pushing and inspect provider feedback to
confirm the intended skip. Configuration validity alone does not prove that Vercel
honored the branch rule. No provider account, production-branch or billing setting is
changed by this repository rule.
# Architecture

## Engine choice

[PixiJS](https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/components/application) supplies the WebGL renderer and scene graph. The game does not need a rigid-body physics engine, a tile map, or an entity framework: the recovered simulation uses authored tank parts, point-against-art collision, independent velocity axes, and frame timers. Keeping those rules in plain TypeScript avoids coupling them to a framework's physics or variable-time integration.

Next.js supplies the application shell, TypeScript build, and static delivery. Tailwind is installed through its PostCSS integration; stage-specific styling is kept in one stylesheet so original Flash coordinates can remain explicit. Pixi is imported on demand by rendered screens. No server-side game API or database is required.

## Ownership and flow

1. `AssetGate` accepts a local file or initializes procedural mock artwork.
2. `AssetPack` extracts images, sounds, vectors, font outlines, and sprite placements. It composes frozen previews and shared vector-leaf textures. It never executes ABC/ActionScript or calls retired endpoints.
3. `GameShell` owns the local profile, screen navigation, dialogs, and a `World` instance.
4. `GameViewport` owns input listeners, the Pixi renderer and cleanup. `MainStage` drives the shared `StageRuntime` fixed-step clock. Input is cleared on blur and gameplay pauses when hidden.
5. `World.step` advances one original game frame. `weapons.ts`, `projectiles.ts`, `actor-movement.ts`, `waves.ts`, and `tank.ts` implement separate systems. Beam contact, healer patient ownership, turret construction, and status callbacks/clocks are isolated in `beams.ts`, `healing.ts`, `turrets.ts`, and `status.ts`. Rendering and browser storage are absent from these rules.
6. `GameRenderer` positions the camera at the avatar, draws fields/entities/projectiles/pickups/effects, and updates `SwfSymbolView` display lists. `AssetPack` supplies matching animated alpha-mask hit tests.
7. React observes a revision counter, approximately ten updates per second at 50 FPS; it does not render every simulation frame.

`MainMenuMotion` belongs to each menu instance and advances on the shared `StageRuntime`. `MainMenuView` retains the supplied-SWF title and control clip trees through Settings/Credits visits; A stage-wide `MenuPointer` queries native retained geometry or procedural contours; DOM buttons retain keyboard access over the canvas. Per-frame rendering uses refs and stage subscriptions, while `GameShell` owns screen changes and the guarded overlay. A new menu instance resets its intro; closing a child pane preserves its title timeline.

The browser-owned `UpgradeMenu` service retains its pure motion model and captured
bitmap history across creator/viewer children. `World.onUpgradeMenuOpen` reports the

`placeUpgrade` synchronously, then presentation completion calls `finishUpgrade`;
direct creator returns use the progression-slot rule. Components observe the shared
service for paint and input state. [Frame ownership](upgrade-frame-reference.md)
documents fresh browser capture and the fixed cohort shared across Main, background
and child-menu phases. Main4 skips World.Run while attached artwork still advances;
explicit World events own background stop/resume independently of dialog mode.

`TankCreator.onLoad` passes its avatar/enemy mode and current limits to the local `TankViewer` screen. `GameShell` retains the editor return context and paused game viewport through that visit; the viewer's artwork and fades use the same stage clock. Selection constructs a fresh editor from the chosen design. Back reconstructs the current avatar or a new empty enemy, matching the recovered source routes. Viewer save/delete callbacks update the versioned local profile, and only completing the final guide page persists `tankViewerHelpSeen`. The viewer handles unavailable community search through the isolated service adapter.

The fixed stage wrappers clip overflow without becoming browser scroll containers, preserving the shared550×450 origin even when retained artwork extends beyond it. Creator input passes physical player coordinates through `core/display-transform.ts`: float32 matrices, signed twip translations, device-pixel mouse rounding, and the event-target/stage/reference Point conversions. The browser supplies the applied CSS transform and DPR; the numeric module has no DOM or saved-data access. `EditorDisplayState` separately owns transient clip x/y/rotation/scale. Drawing, hit tests, selection bounds and radial validation consume those getters, while tank codes and history retain raw saved fields. Drag membership/twin links update during movement and selected positions synchronize on release; each transform handle releases only its own field. Nudging advances both stores independently per frame; undo and rejected edits reconstruct clips from accepted metadata. Class measurement separately constructs its source snapshot from saved fields through display setters.

Marquee paint and its retained source flag have different lifetimes. The first release clears the rectangle; later editor mouse-ups still run `_‑bp` until a workspace click or `_‑JQ` rebind clears the flag. Selection samples combine clip positions with saved radius/scale, and the actual release point is independent of the last drawn rectangle. The earlier stage listener can clear selection before a slider's stage release copies its field. Delete instead acts at target mouse-up, while layering/centering and the extra nudge pixel act on the later click. Selection controls remain mounted while hidden, retaining that click and its accepted no-op history entry. Held nudge history is recorded before that click. Palette dragging and scrollbar dragging detach/rebind the workspace listener. Live selection refs preserve this ordering within a React event; the same native event is consumed once. Accessible range changes commit immediately and clear the retained marquee state. Workspace/transform cancellation restores the preceding gesture state and suppresses its trailing release.

Attached status marks are simulation state: their chosen part positions, rotations, variants, and replacement lifetime stay stable across frames and inactive fields. `SwfTankStatusView` consumes those choices without drawing random values or changing game rules. It holds variant frames while allowing nested clips to animate and applies the recovered infection color matrix to the complete tank view. Screen ink is an independently queued global effect; its lifetime and overlap do not belong to an avatar.

`assets/sound-window.ts` decodes native MP3 at its tag rate before AssetPack becomes ready, crops the positive source seek/sample-count window and prepares local16-bit PCM WAV blobs. Browser decoding stays outside simulation. `AudioManager` consumes events through its ten general sound slots and advances music from the shared stage before World steps, retaining source transition acceptance and muted-track memory. Fresh menu/game construction issues a distinct music request; profile settings only change enablement. Retained Settings, creator and nested viewer visits do not invent scene requests. Music completion restarts the same media carrier at full source volume without resetting the stage transition counter; replaced, muted and disposed voices cannot restart through stale callbacks. `simulation/collision-sound.ts` dispatches the recovered virtual hit-sound policy and callback enemy argument; World advances its shared hit cooldown at the successful Run tail, including pause. An interrupted listener skips that tail. The browser does not apply a second hit throttle.

`simulation/damage.ts` owns integer coercion, weaken, shield/forcefield absorption, recursive overflow, life changes, and the player hurt-channel latch. The latch advances with tank Run frames, independent of browser audio. `simulation/degradation.ts` owns the original incremental body-loss state (debt, total and cached minimum), keeping its selection order and healing behavior separate from rendering. Player bodies remain visible; surviving enemies/allies degrade, while enemy healing restores visibility before another degradation call. Both alpha collision and `TankView` consume the resulting hidden-part set.

The active frame checks progression in the interface phase, after existing-avatar controls/HUD and before field combat. Ordinary upgrades/downgrades therefore observe the previous field frame's final health. Level-zero damage starts its escape immediately. Primary input and passive weapons use separate category passes through `tickGuns`; passive shots are born after the field's bullet loop. Primary triggers run before field combat; primary cooldowns/aim and passive firing run in the later avatar phase. HUD readouts are captured in the interface phase, so later health/counter changes cannot leak into the same displayed frame. Shared secondary readiness retains its distinct zero reset frame and advances during transit. `WorldFlow` keeps raw execution state and its shared saved return state separate from attached dialogs. The selected Run branch finishes even when its interface opens a menu; crossing arrival can therefore restore state2 with a missing destination, while secondary-help Close writes ordinary state0 with its attachment still pending. The known source listener boundaries preserve those outcomes; browser mid-crossing pause is a separate existing adapter. Boundary detection precedes interface work; the initiating state0 frame still runs the avatar, while subsequent state2 frames run both fields without player status/passive updates. Arrival clears movement and the player shield, discards all registered effects/callbacks, and resets primary counters. The fidelity ledger identifies remaining source quirks, weapon callbacks and independent animation-clock work.

`simulation/field-runtime.ts` owns each live wrapper's shots, pickups, allies, removal queues and pending effects. `FieldCache` holds ordered actor references with frozen pose scalars, including raw queued deaths; attachment restores them into a fresh wrapper and replaces their parent/callback ownership. Logical map coordinates advance at attachment, separately from the current displayed field. The current and latest next wrapper receive combat Run; superseded next wrappers retain their last stage pose and independent artwork. `attachedFields()` exposes that display ownership separately from `activeFields()`. Completed outgoing wrappers clear shots/pickups before detachment; uncleared wrappers retain their detached collections. The destination keeps its already-running collections. Global effect clearing remains separate. A nested synchronous field context projects the same avatar and restores it with `try/finally`; world-level escape markers use current-wrapper coordinates even when next-field damage initiates the callback. Enemy and ally removal queues flush at the next field frame. Reparenting does not erase old array references or transfer an already queued callback. The live bullet loop still processes newly appended fragments in the same frame. See [crossing source contracts](crossing-source-reference.md).

`simulation/player-direction.ts` separates interface direction from acceleration and translation. It preserves the recovered heavy-tank turn helper, including exact-opposite ties, and updates aim/steering during transit without enabling movement.

`simulation/wall-timers.ts` models elapsed-millisecond Flash Timer callbacks separately from fixed-step part counters. The production viewport advances it from actual RAF elapsed time and passes zero elapsed milliseconds into each fixed stage step; deterministic callers can use `World.step(input, milliseconds)` (default20ms). The player launcher starts ten100ms callbacks; ordinary crossings and avatar replacement cancel them, while pause/jam/stun and death escape do not. Transit rejects insertion without replaying consumed callbacks. Managed Massive Cannon/shield timelines advance once per stage step even while paused, loop at their authored length, and are polled only by active world modes. Completion follows field bullets. This models source lifecycle; exact Flash Timer/event-loop delivery under stalls remains a runtime comparison boundary.

`simulation/pickups.ts` owns denomination selection, initial scatter, attraction and collection. Pickup state keeps scattering and the near-center collection latch separate from completion's forced attraction. The field performs alpha/latch collection before motion, preserves the original live-vector removal behavior, and advances its own collection sound counter after completion. Bounds deliberately consult the outgoing wrapper during transit, matching the source. `weapon-cycles.ts` stores the two special enemy firing cycles on each mounted gun, so jam/stun pauses their counters independently of visual age.

Non-player actors advance movement/sticky, jam, ordered parts, protection/effects, then ink/infection/weaken and boundary checks. NPC damage death and allied direct boundary exit share a deactivation phase in `World`: primary final callbacks run while data is live, before clearing data, setting the dead flag and recording the owning field callback. Damage supplies side-specific sounds/drops/infection before that phase; allied boundary exit supplies drops/pop and bypasses damage protection. Enemy callbacks queue next-frame removal; existing ally filtering retains its start/end timing. A stunned entry skips movement, parts and boundary for its complete reset frame while keeping protection/effects active. Enemy and ally arrays run independently without snapshots, allowing newly spawned enemies to run immediately. Player interface/passive ordering remains separate and its remaining source differences are tracked in the fidelity ledger.

`render/tank-view.ts` paints a runtime tank independently of camera and simulation clocks. The game renderer and `TankPortrait` use it for the same current mounted-part rotations, visibility, animation pose, status and protection. The portrait owns a temporary transparent Pixi canvas above the paused field, at the original tank scale. Leaving the screen destroys that canvas and its texture store. `core/tank-info.ts` supplies source class/weapon formatting and frame-based entrance/retraction; its placements, TextField metrics and font ascent come from the HUD importer. Info does not export a reconstructed static design in place of the current pose.

`core/win-screen.ts` supplies the source preparation/fade clock independently of gameplay. `WinPanel` consumes static text/art and button frames loaded into `AssetPack.uiFrames`; it has no invented statistics. `tools/import-win-geometry.ts` preserves authored positions and alpha values while filtering the retired pack-manager promotion. The separate visual-fixture viewer mounts the production panel for browser checks. The clock records original blur-pass timing, but shared CSS blur still approximates the original repeated BitmapData filtering.

## Invariants

- Simulation units are pixels/frame, degrees, and frame counters. Do not multiply recovered constants by wall-clock delta.
- The stage is 550 × 450; rendering scales to fit without changing world dimensions.
- Health and progression are the same resource. Kills alone do not grant XP.
- The level life curve is `[50, 100, 170, 250, 400, 800, 2000]`.
- Mounted primary cooldowns are independent; secondaries share their maximum mounted rate.
- Field persistence owns living enemies and their exact runtime state. Inactive fields do not keep simulating.
- Recovered catalog designs are immutable templates. Runtime health, timers, removed carrier parts, and hidden bubbles live on `Tank` instances.
- Flash artwork is optional input. Mock mode must remain playable without a file.
- Map connections are completed traversal history, independent of grid adjacency and field generation. Each unordered pair is stored once. Cleared fields remain valid destinations.
- Camera zoom changes renderer scale and inverse pointer mapping together; simulation coordinates and the fixed HUD keep their original dimensions.

## Extending the game

- Add a part definition in the catalog, an implementation in the relevant combat/AI system, and a recovered symbol or mock view. Keep part IDs stable for code compatibility.
- Keep data importers reproducible. Derived JSON is checked in so the research repository is not a production dependency.
- `services/extensions.ts` contains typed interfaces for community tanks, accounts, parts packs, medals, platform stats, and ads. Replace the offline adapters to restore those systems without adding endpoint logic to gameplay.
- `services/profile.ts` validates versioned local JSON. The persistence boundary is replaceable; no component needs to know Flash SharedObject internals.
- `services/tank-code.ts` implements the original AES-128-ECB/PKCS7 tank format using Web Crypto's CBC primitive blockwise. It is a compatibility codec, not an account/security mechanism.
- A future renderer can consume the same `World`; a replay/test harness can call `World.step` with seeded input without a DOM.

## Asset lifetime

`Tank.age` follows active actor Run. `Tank.artAge` follows attached stage frames, including pause, control suspension and the avatar during travel. `simulation/tank-art.ts` advances artwork for the player and both attached field populations once; cached inactive fields do not advance. Native painting, part alpha tests, status/infection visual origins and forcefield mask clips use that stage age. Status durations, infection damage, weapon counters and forcefield recharge retain their active clocks. Shield film has26 frames independently of its25-frame cleanup callback; shield hits stop at16 and can finish after immunity ends. Forcefield frame jumps follow the authored1/25/35 scripts on the stage clock.

`core/protection-size.ts` preserves TankData's ordered axis-record algorithm, including ties and all-centered NaN. The browser binds `World.protectionRadius` to `AssetPack`'s transformed live Script bounds; headless callers can inject geometry, with stored-radius estimates as the default. A shield mount caches its first measured diameter, while the current hit clip retains the last mount-created diameter. `AssetPack` separately creates a fresh full-design forcefield mask pose tree and caches its initial sizing before stage advancement. Native width/height NaN assignments retain authored scale; forcefield sizing uses uniform width scale. Turret shields keep the separate gameplay-radius rule. Mock parts supply procedural raster dimensions to the same ordering rule.

The supplied SWF is held only for extraction. Projectile and pickup display lists share the same vector textures as tank views. Music fades advance on the shared stage clock, including in menus and while gameplay is paused. Audio Blob URLs are owned and revoked by `AudioManager`. Pixi textures and display trees are owned by `GameRenderer`; changing files, leaving a run, and unmounting remove listeners and release rendering resources. The asset pack keeps shared raster/font/timeline caches for the current selected file and clears them when replaced.

The shell owns a reactive audio-manager instance so the viewport receives the loaded pack's audio service. Pointer/key gestures retry suspended music on the current element. Mock audio is generated locally as short PCM WAVs, including a quiet music loop, and uses the same channel limits, mute controls, and cleanup as supplied SWF audio. Protection views use shared vector leaves and a cloned design mask; changing a design rebuilds its cached tank view.

The parser was adapted from `research/swf-browser-extraction/`. Corrections made here cover matrix byte alignment and shear order, `PlaceObject3` flags, retained color transforms and removal events, shape pen origins, appended style tables and paint layers, joined fill boundaries, normalized SVG view boxes, font outlines/advances, and masked sprite composition. Matrix semantics were cross-checked against [FFDec's input reader](https://github.com/jindrapetrik/jpexs-decompiler/blob/master/libsrc/ffdec_lib/src/com/jpexs/decompiler/flash/SWFInputStream.java) and [affine transform implementation](https://github.com/jindrapetrik/jpexs-decompiler/blob/master/libsrc/ffdec_lib/src/com/jpexs/decompiler/flash/exporters/commonshape/Matrix.java).

Morph placements retain their unsigned 16-bit ratio. `morphShapeAtRatio` resolves geometry, bounds, colors, gradient matrices/stops/focal values, and line widths; previews and collision use the same resolved geometry as live views. `morph-raster.ts` rasterizes generated leaf paths synchronously with Canvas2D so frame changes do not wait for image decoding. Its recent-raster cache is limited to eight million pixels. Live morph textures are reference counted by `GameRenderer` and released when their last view changes ratio or is destroyed; static vector leaves remain shared for the run. Morph structure and edge pairing were cross-checked against [FFDec's morph implementation](https://github.com/jindrapetrik/jpexs-decompiler/blob/master/libsrc/ffdec_lib/src/com/jpexs/decompiler/flash/tags/base/MorphShapeTag.java).

`tools/visual-fixtures.ts` builds a separate development viewer with deterministic world snapshots. It uses the production asset pack, simulation, and renderer; native SWF loading remains local. Browser tests compare contact masks and construction states there without adding debug routes or globals to the shipped application.

`simulation/editor-selection.ts` contains pure creator operations: ordered additive selections, faded twin membership, marquee sampling, transforms, ordering, and unlink/delete behavior. `simulation/editor-validation.ts` owns source-ordered aggregate checks against explicit class/budget values. `simulation/editor-history.ts` retains independent accepted part snapshots, including setup/import and accepted no-op operations; enemy statistics remain outside undo. `TankCreator` owns pointer capture, transient drag state, class-update timing and drawing. Selection and faded state are never exported as tank data. Browser coverage reads nonvisual design metadata after actual pointer interactions in both asset modes.

Prepared native creator819 background frames apply a scoped minimum-stroke width through the verified positive uniform placement tree. They paint in a registered decorative image behind the input/part canvas so the two-pixel raster padding preserves the complete border. This adapter leaves authored geometry, ordinary SVG/raster calls and Script/contact bounds unchanged; it does not model Ruffle tessellation-cache history.

`simulation/editor-drag.ts` advances a creator drag one pointer event at a time. It owns per-part pointer sides, the first-move reference offset, the axis lock, merge/delete decisions, and new mirrored twin insertion. Each advance returns new parts and selection state without mutating its input. The component starts on the first delivered move event without a displacement threshold, including zero delta; only a press with no move event retains ordinary click selection toggling. It retains the source's axis-lock flag across gestures, records accepted drag releases including no-op snapshots, and restores the starting design/selection on pointer cancellation. Browser coordinate arithmetic does not yet reproduce every original Point/display-setter precision boundary.

`simulation/editor-placement.ts` creates transient preview geometry, applies the three-pixel axis snap, and filters each dropped member against the design bounds. Palette choice, the in-progress preview gesture, and selection of placed parts are separate editor states. The browser component owns pointer capture and the keyboard alternative; dropping an object commits one design change without selecting it. Part radii come from authored symbol bounds, excluding the raster padding used for antialiasing.

`tools/reference-player.ts` serves a separate loopback-only original SWF viewer with development dependency Ruffle 0.7.1. It shares the SWF decompressor, serves WASM with the correct MIME type, and accepts a browser-local file or explicit `BT3_SWF_FILE`. `reference-browser.ts` owns a headless Chrome/CDP instance with the stack size this movie needs; `reference-input.ts` uses Node Playwright for native coordinate input and stage captures. Ruffle is never imported by `src` or included in the Next.js output. The optional original-runtime smoke test is enabled with `BT3_REFERENCE=1`; it complements simulation tests rather than establishing whole-game parity.

`simulation/editor-palette.ts` owns affordability, unlock state, source row ordering, and default selection independently of placement. Affordability checks one object; symmetry and final design validity are handled by placement and save validation. An unaffordable unlocked row is dimmed but remains selectable.

`render/creator-artwork.ts` reuses `SwfSymbolView` in one offscreen Pixi renderer, copying its transparent frame into the creator's design and preview canvases. Each placed part owns its own timeline birth frame; moving/scaling/selecting it does not recreate the clip. Dropping transfers draft views into the design so their animation continues. The frame clock follows the selected FPS, stops advancing while hidden, and stays outside React state. Pointer alpha tests consume each part's retained visible pose. Class measurement and saved designs continue to use their separate static snapshot and numerical geometry.

`CreatorArtwork` also owns an independent details layer. It measures a fresh clip before animation, caps its dominant dimension at48px once, and retains that scale through subsequent frames. Clearing the layer destroys its clips so a new detail focus restarts construction. Full-size palette previews retain their own instances and scale. Supplied-SWF loading caches the details static panel, both arrow poses, selection icon and popup; named fields and dynamic children remain outside these static rasters. The live part-details component uses these caches; selection-info UI uses the same retained cache.

`render/swf-textures.ts` owns leaf textures and reference-counted morph textures for both the game and creator renderers. Each renderer has its own store and releases it with its display trees. No animation frame atlas is generated, and closing the creator cancels its frame callback and destroys its offscreen WebGL resources.

`assets/clip-timeline.ts` runs the recovered stop, jump, rounded-random, and Y-branch actions. `assets/swf-clip.ts` owns the retained child tree and advances every elapsed stage frame, including child construction/removal while a parent is stopped. It has no DOM or Pixi dependency. `SwfSymbolView.updatePose` paints that tree; collision reads the same placements, masks, and morph ratios through `AssetPack.hitClip`.

`assets/glow-kernel.ts` and `assets/swf-color-transform.ts` hold numeric filter rules independently of Pixi. `SwfSymbolView` retains each placement's ordered glow filters, isolates authored bitmap-cache boundaries, and applies accumulated color after a filtered capture. Unfiltered branches pass color to their leaves. Embedding views supply runtime/parent alpha explicitly so Pixi ancestors do not attenuate the capture. `SwfGlowFilter` owns the repeated horizontal/vertical GPU passes and pooled scratch textures; `SwfColorFilter` applies the final bitmap transform. Contact and Script bounds retain their separate geometry. The development-only byte-image oracle and gallery test the rendering without entering the shipped game bundle.

`AssetPack.partClip` caches poses in a weak map keyed by runtime tank and resets them when its design changes. Each part has a stable private random stream derived from the tank/instance key, so repeated rendering or collision queries do not reroll animation or consume gameplay randomness. Creator clips use their own retained instances and normal random draws; the forcefield's cloned silhouette also owns independent instances. Numeric frame actions are generated from complete recognized source methods. Unsupported classes are reported, and importing fails if an unsupported frame method becomes reachable from a catalog part.

`core/minimap.ts` holds the imported layout and the compact/large/hidden state helpers. `render/minimap-view.ts` owns the native map shell, retained dot clips, traversal graphics, and clipping; it sits outside the world camera transform. Entries detach before an authored frame swap so replacing `map_mc` cannot destroy retained traversal artwork. The mock renderer follows the same control cycle and spacing. `WorldMap` supplies only the accessible cycle button and a screen-reader description; opening the map does not create a dialog or pause the simulation.

`core/hud.ts` owns health/fire idle clocks and easing in original simulation frames, ordered primary grouping, and fill calculations. `render/hud-view.ts` owns the native life/fire clip trees and their dynamic device-text children; mock mode draws the corresponding simple geometry. Both stay outside the camera transform. `GameHud` retains accessible health text and interactive controls, without React updates or CSS transitions driving the bar animation. `tools/import-hud-geometry.ts` imports only numerical origins, layout heights, and TextField metrics from the source SWF; artwork remains browser-local.

`core/edit-slider.ts` advances the source's distance-scaled entrance/retraction in simulation frames. Completion and field attachment trigger it; a settled tab reflows when the map changes size. `render/edit-slider-view.ts` paints the three native variants, including static text leaves. `EditTankControl` reads the model to move its transparent native-button bounds without React frame updates. Its DOM disabled state follows the model; React does not hold a conflicting fixed disabled prop. Clicking opens the original confirmation, then same-level replacement choices. Editing or selecting a replacement rebuilds the current progression slot at its initial health; canceling the creator resumes the run.

`core/tutorial.ts` selects a stopped caption frame using the unique-field count before attachment increments it. Every attachment, including a revisit, replaces the destination's guide. `render/field-captions.ts` retains the original static text/logo clip for each active field, below tanks, with no field-radius scaling. The field camera moves it through crossings; pausing does not remove the artwork. `tools/import-tutorial-art.ts` imports frame IDs, numerical positions and decoded fallback text. The original glyphs, colors and font outlines come from the supplied SWF. Mock mode spells out the separate W and mouse glyphs in readable fallback text.

`core/field-visit.ts` models the per-attachment completion latch independently of cached `Field.cleared`. `World` owns one current visit and a fresh destination visit during transit, checking both in source order and transferring the latch on arrival. Empty revisits increment completion statistics once per attachment without adding duplicate map paths. The initial wrapper is special; attaching home again is an ordinary visit.

`World.rebuildPlayer` owns the replacement-only secondary-help trigger and early seen latch. `GameShell` persists that event in the validated local profile; initial saved-avatar construction does not trigger it. A dedicated world mode freezes simulation while `SecondaryHelpPanel` displays the original static artwork and button frames loaded by `AssetPack.uiFrames`. Its generated placement data shares the HUD importer; the regular modal scrim is disabled so the authored white veil remains intact.

`core/tactical-hud.ts` holds fixed-stage snapshots for Radar, Health Readout and allied health. Their clocks differ: the interface updates ally rings through travel, while avatar passive parts retain their last snapshot until active again. Jam clears passive output and stun retains it. `render/tactical-hud-view.ts` paints native116/1999/2194 clips outside the camera, overwriting enemy fill scale and preserving source widths/heights. `core/target-lock.ts` defines the disabled parts-pack targeting boundary. No shipped part registers locks, and base Q input does not alter homing or auto-cannon targeting. `simulation/effects.ts` maps projectile callbacks to source effect identities independently of damage. `tools/import-effect-art.ts` regenerates their symbol IDs and frame counts without exporting artwork. Each field owns an effect request queue, flushed after its combat, pickups and completion checks. Arrival clears registered clips and callbacks. Effect ages advance on the stage clock even while gameplay is paused, while engine polling removes clips only on active gameplay/collapse frames. `render/combat-effects-view.ts` owns lower, upper and screen native effect containers and shared-texture MovieClip trees. Mock mode draws the same segment with a procedural fade and uses simple rings for the other source-defined effects. Ordinary damage/death and area damage do not independently create visual effects. Native artwork remains runtime SWF input, including all 12 newly reachable effect roots.

`simulation/projectile-contact.ts` handles the base current/backward-half-step mask tests and Massive Cannon's cardinal width samples before movement. It retains the friendly enemy-layer gate and source hit-memory behavior. Collision callbacks run before direct damage and can create effects, pickups or area damage independently. `tools/import-projectile-flags.ts` recovers constructor flags through source inheritance into `data/projectile-flags.json`; acquisition and area cleanup use those flags instead of inferring behavior from projectile kind. It selects the first enemy clip in live array order using strict distance and Script width; later Busters may overwrite the same vector. Subtype aiming/contact/fuse polls stop, while retained stage artwork continues. Movement precedes the virtual wall check, which is skipped for stopped turrets (the shipped live `_‑PJ=false` case). Beams never expire at this boundary, ricochets expire without bouncing or reporting a miss, and Apocalypse uses the stroke-inclusive background radius425.25 rather than its fill radius423.75. Turret Setup initializes its movement before its first interception; interception uses copied vectors for deflected incoming shots, and owner validity follows field attachment rather than the death flag. Infection's shipped NaN acquisition failure is explicit in `infection-projectile.ts`; setup and first-Run effects/removal use the regular field queue. Leech creates a forced value1 pickup, leaving movement, collection accounting and healing to the pickup system.

`assets/projectile-bounds.ts` composes native leaf transforms into field-coordinate Script AABBs independently of raster painting. It retains mask/transparent children, declared morph start bounds, dynamic beam lengths and turret orientation. `GameViewport` binds `World.projectileBounds` to the supplied asset pack; width-based Massive Cannon/Buster checks derive from that same bound. # Architecture

## Engine choice

[PixiJS](https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/components/application) supplies the WebGL renderer and scene graph. The game does not need a rigid-body physics engine, a tile map, or an entity framework: the recovered simulation uses authored tank parts, point-against-art collision, independent velocity axes, and frame timers. Keeping those rules in plain TypeScript avoids coupling them to a framework's physics or variable-time integration.

Next.js supplies the application shell, TypeScript build, and static delivery. Tailwind is installed through its PostCSS integration; stage-specific styling is kept in one stylesheet so original Flash coordinates can remain explicit. Pixi is imported on demand by rendered screens. No server-side game API or database is required.

## Ownership and flow

1. `AssetGate` accepts a local file or initializes procedural mock artwork.
2. `AssetPack` extracts images, sounds, vectors, font outlines, and sprite placements. It composes frozen previews and shared vector-leaf textures. It never executes ABC/ActionScript or calls retired endpoints.
3. `GameShell` owns the local profile, screen navigation, dialogs, and a `World` instance.
4. `GameViewport` owns input listeners, the Pixi renderer and cleanup. `MainStage` drives the shared `StageRuntime` fixed-step clock. Input is cleared on blur and gameplay pauses when hidden.
5. `World.step` advances one original game frame. `weapons.ts`, `projectiles.ts`, `actor-movement.ts`, `waves.ts`, and `tank.ts` implement separate systems. Beam contact, healer patient ownership, turret construction, and status callbacks/clocks are isolated in `beams.ts`, `healing.ts`, `turrets.ts`, and `status.ts`. Rendering and browser storage are absent from these rules.
6. `GameRenderer` positions the camera at the avatar, draws fields/entities/projectiles/pickups/effects, and updates `SwfSymbolView` display lists. `AssetPack` supplies matching animated alpha-mask hit tests.
7. React observes a revision counter, approximately ten updates per second at 50 FPS; it does not render every simulation frame.

`MainMenuMotion` belongs to each menu instance and advances on the shared `StageRuntime`. `MainMenuView` retains the supplied-SWF title and control clip trees through Settings/Credits visits; A stage-wide `MenuPointer` queries native retained geometry or procedural contours; DOM buttons retain keyboard access over the canvas. Per-frame rendering uses refs and stage subscriptions, while `GameShell` owns screen changes and the guarded overlay. A new menu instance resets its intro; closing a child pane preserves its title timeline.

The browser-owned `UpgradeMenu` service retains its pure motion model and captured
bitmap history across creator/viewer children. `World.onUpgradeMenuOpen` reports the
interface-phase opening without storing browser objects. Card selection calls
`placeUpgrade` synchronously, then presentation completion calls `finishUpgrade`;
direct creator returns use the progression-slot rule. Components observe the shared
service for paint and input state. [Frame ownership](upgrade-frame-reference.md)
documents fresh browser capture and the fixed cohort shared across Main, background
and child-menu phases. Main4 skips World.Run while attached artwork still advances;
explicit World events own background stop/resume independently of dialog mode.

`TankCreator.onLoad` passes its avatar/enemy mode and current limits to the local `TankViewer` screen. `GameShell` retains the editor return context and paused game viewport through that visit; the viewer's artwork and fades use the same stage clock. Selection constructs a fresh editor from the chosen design. Back reconstructs the current avatar or a new empty enemy, matching the recovered source routes. Viewer save/delete callbacks update the versioned local profile, and only completing the final guide page persists `tankViewerHelpSeen`. The viewer handles unavailable community search through the isolated service adapter.

The fixed stage wrappers clip overflow without becoming browser scroll containers, preserving the shared550×450 origin even when retained artwork extends beyond it. A primary creator workspace press closes Enemy Info while retaining its manual values. Dialog buttons remain text-only state layers: the native raster API has no static artwork to cache for their up/over/down records.

Creator input passes physical player coordinates through `core/display-transform.ts`: float32 matrices, signed twip translations, device-pixel mouse rounding, and the event-target/stage/reference Point conversions. The browser supplies the applied CSS transform and DPR; the numeric module has no DOM or saved-data access. `EditorDisplayState` separately owns transient clip x/y/rotation/scale. Drawing, hit tests, selection bounds and radial validation consume those getters, while tank codes and history retain raw saved fields. Drag membership/twin links update during movement and selected positions synchronize on release; each transform handle releases only its own field. Nudging advances both stores independently per frame; undo and rejected edits reconstruct clips from accepted metadata. Class measurement separately constructs its source snapshot from saved fields through display setters.

Marquee paint and its retained source flag have different lifetimes. ## Invariants

- Simulation units are pixels/frame, degrees, and frame counters. Do not multiply recovered constants by wall-clock delta.
- The stage is 550 × 450; rendering scales to fit without changing world dimensions.
- Health and progression are the same resource. Kills alone do not grant XP.
- The level life curve is `[50, 100, 170, 250, 400, 800, 2000]`.
- Mounted primary cooldowns are independent; secondaries share their maximum mounted rate.
- Field persistence owns living enemies and their exact runtime state. Inactive fields do not keep simulating.
- Recovered catalog designs are immutable templates. Runtime health, timers, removed carrier parts, and hidden bubbles live on `Tank` instances.
- Flash artwork is optional input. Mock mode must remain playable without a file.
- Map connections are completed traversal history, independent of grid adjacency and field generation. Each unordered pair is stored once. Cleared fields remain valid destinations.
- Camera zoom changes renderer scale and inverse pointer mapping together; simulation coordinates and the fixed HUD keep their original dimensions.

## Extending the game

- Add a part definition in the catalog, an implementation in the relevant combat/AI system, and a recovered symbol or mock view. Keep part IDs stable for code compatibility.
- Keep data importers reproducible. Derived JSON is checked in so the research repository is not a production dependency.
- `services/extensions.ts` contains typed interfaces for community tanks, accounts, parts packs, medals, platform stats, and ads. Replace the offline adapters to restore those systems without adding endpoint logic to gameplay.
- `services/profile.ts` validates versioned local JSON. The persistence boundary is replaceable; no component needs to know Flash SharedObject internals.
- `services/tank-code.ts` implements the original AES-128-ECB/PKCS7 tank format using Web Crypto's CBC primitive blockwise. It is a compatibility codec, not an account/security mechanism.
- A future renderer can consume the same `World`; a replay/test harness can call `World.step` with seeded input without a DOM.

## Asset lifetime

The browser binds `World.protectionRadius` to `AssetPack`'s transformed live Script bounds; headless callers can inject geometry, with stored-radius estimates as the default. ```text
accepted projectile birth
  prepare final position
  apply signed-twip display writes
  run virtual Setup
per-frame movement
  preserve private Number vectors
  apply each source X/Y display write
carrier launch
  convert emitter into outgoing field
  add six field-axis offsets
  initialize each seeker from its final position

- **Before:** Nine shared-movement, fifteen birth/custom-write and three carrier regressions fail against their respective preceding source snapshots.   **After:** Formatting, TypeScript and 960 unit tests / 8,659 assertions pass. **Door:** two-way

Position quantization affects movement, homing initialization, mines, maintained beams and turret damping. Collision/phase order and private vector precision remain separate. Absent Vercel status is not proof of a provider-confirmed skip.

# REA

Use REA when a claim depends on a shipped binary or package, decompilation,
passive application runtime evidence, or comparison with
behavior not established by available source. For ordinary analysis of a
complete source repository, use normal repository tools and do not run REA
readiness or provider commands.

## Connect only when needed

Installing this skill supplies instructions; it does not register the REA MCP
server, install analysis engines, or add tools to an already-running agent.

If REA tools are available and their registration is not known to be stale,
proceed directly to the target. Do not run diagnostics or setup before every
investigation. Use the connected server's actual tool list and input schemas;
a skill installed from repository main may describe capabilities absent from
an older npm release. Keep complete inline Evidence when that server does not
advertise retained references.

If tools are absent, a call is blocked by the client, or a required provider is
unavailable, read [connection and recovery](references/connection-and-recovery.md).
Diagnose the observed blocker, continue useful supported work, and resume the
original task after repair. Client approval, shell PATH, registration and engine
availability have different remedies; avoid repeating setup for all of them.

1. Diagnose without changing REA or client configuration. `npx` may download
   the package and write to npm's cache. For Codex, run
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 doctor --client codex --json`. Substitute the current
   supported client: `claude_code`, `claude_desktop`, `codex`, `cursor`,
   `gemini_cli`, `windsurf`, `devin`, `opencode`, `antigravity`, `copilot_cli`,
   `commandcode`, `vscode`, `grok_build`, `omp`, or `grok_bot`. `grok_bot` has no local
   file registration: doctor reports the Grok Bot chat step, and setup does not
   write `mcp.json`. If the client is unknown, use `doctor --json` and
   inspect its registration results before choosing a setup scope.
2. Distinguish the reason. Missing, malformed, or stale registration needs a
   scoped configuration repair. An aligned registration with no tools in the
   active session needs a restart/reconnection; doctor cannot prove that the
   current agent has connected. A missing provider affects only tasks requiring
   that provider: static JavaScript inspection needs neither Hopper nor Ghidra,
   and Android inspection has separate bring-your-own JADX/Java prerequisites.
3. For a configuration repair, prepare the read-only plan:
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 setup --client codex --dry-run --json`.
   Use the current client's ID, show its exact proposed paths, backups, and
   changes, and obtain approval before setup writes configuration or installs
   Hopper. Setup normally installs the matching bundled skill too; include that
   replacement in the reviewed plan. After approval, apply the same scope with
   `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 setup --client codex --yes`. Add `--install-hopper`
   only if that separate installation was needed and explicitly approved.
4. Restart/reconnect the affected agent. Verify that REA tools actually appear
   in the session, then resume the original investigation. If they remain
   absent, inspect the client's MCP launch error rather than repeating setup.

REA setup never installs or upgrades Node.js, npm, Homebrew, Java, Ghidra, IDA,
JADX, Kuna, Binwalk, or Unblob. Use existing prerequisites; do not install unrelated
software to repair
MCP registration. For an unsupported client, use manual stdio registration
with a version-pinned `rea-agents` package or continue through the CLI.

A concrete CLI fallback for an operator-supplied JavaScript tree or ASAR is:

```bash
npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0 analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json
```

No MCP registration or native engine is required. Read the returned Evidence,
graph, limitations, and unknowns with the same care as an MCP result; the CLI
returns the Evidence record directly. This fallback does not establish that
MCP is configured. Native CLI tasks still require their selected engine.
Prefer an existing `rea` CLI. When none is installed and REA package acquisition
is within the authorized scope, use `npx -y rea-agents@6.7.0` in its place.
Configuration repair starts with a read-only setup plan; show paths, backups and
skill replacement before applying authorized changes. Preserve existing approval
and target-execution boundaries. REA setup never installs or upgrades unrelated
software, including Node.js, npm, Homebrew, Java, Ghidra, IDA, JADX, Kuna, Binwalk or Unblob.

## Route the target first

Choose the first tool from the target the user supplied. Use `open_binary` for
active-target native or archive workflows; target-free tools take their own
explicit path or endpoint and do not need it.

- ASAR or extracted JavaScript/Electron tree:
  `analyze_javascript_application`.
- Archive/package member inventory (ZIP/APK/IPA/MSIX/AppX or DMG):
  `open_binary` with the supplied local path; use `inspect_artifact` when its
  graph and findings help answer the question.
- Android APK code, classes, methods, or incoming references:
  `inspect_android_package`, then focused Android tools when advertised.
  Archive member inventory still uses the archive route above.
- Managed PE/CLI assembly: `inspect_managed_artifact`.
- Firmware image: `inspect_firmware_regions` when advertised. Use
  `extract_firmware` when extraction is requested, with a caller-selected new
  absolute output directory. These tools use caller-supplied Binwalk/Unblob on
  Linux; see the [firmware guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/firmware-analysis.md).
- .NET NativeAOT PE/ELF: native Ghidra analysis. Native code can yield pseudocode;
  consult the NativeAOT workflow in `references/native-and-artifacts.md` for
  optional metadata recovery and its supported host/layout boundary.
- User-owned browser page already open: `list_browser_targets`.
- Browser action the agent must perform (click, type, navigate):
  `capture_browser_scenario` with declared actions. See
  [runtime observation](references/runtime-observation.md) for connect/launch
  and the focused follow-up browser tools.
- Fiddler Everywhere traffic or a native `.saz` capture: read the
  [Fiddler workflow](references/runtime-observation.md#fiddler-everywhere-traffic-debugging).
  Inspect saved SAZ with `inspect_web_network_capture` and `format: "saz"`;
  connect Everywhere's separate MCP server for live traffic.
- Retained HAR/SAZ/native mitmproxy/aioquic qlog capture: `inspect_web_network_capture`. Select
  original record ordinals when useful; inspect producer fields and byte/number
  sidecars without fetching recorded URLs or claiming live attribution. See
  [historical captures](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/web-network-captures.md) for the exact upstream
  profile and credential exclusions. Qlog support starts with aioquic 1.5.0
  JSON 0.3; stream coverage and endpoint loss declarations do not recover bodies
  or establish network loss. Prefer detail summary, then kind qlog trace/stream
  pages; select one trace, stream ID and direction for contribution/range pages.
  Facts retain all-recorded-events-before-selection scope. Other qlog layouts
  and PCAP correlation are unsupported.
- User-owned Electron runtime already open: `list_electron_targets`. Before an electron-main Inspector attempt, check packaged fuses with `inspect_electron_fuses`; disabled `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` means the app ignores `--inspect`.
- Packet-field discovery: `inspect_packet_fields` searches installed protocols
  and field names/types before choosing fields for `inspect_packet_capture`.
  Query/page the relevant records; registrations do not establish observed traffic.
- Recorded packet captures: `inspect_packet_capture` with selected TShark fields,
  display filters and decode-as rules. Requires Linux, util-linux prlimit and `REA_TSHARK_COMMAND`; see
  [capture guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/packet-captures.md).
  Packet limits count input packets before filtering. Output defaults to 50 matching
  frames; use `match_offset` / `match_limit` for later pages, or explicit null
  limit for complete matching output. Preserve the source digest across pages.
  This does not perform live capture.
  For address/DNS/SNI/protocol summaries use `inspect_pcap_capture` with MCP
  detail summary, then retained kind pcap pages. Requires Wireshark 4.x tshark
  and capinfos, with Linux prlimit or Windows Job Objects; see
  [packet summaries](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/pcap-analysis.md).
  Select an exact DNS question for address pages; page exhaustion does not prove
  network completeness. This reads recordings and does not acquire traffic.
- Decoder discovery: `inspect_signal_decoders` searches installed decoder IDs
  or selected decoder help, including channels and options. Query and page the
  relevant details before choosing settings; this does not scan hardware.
- Recorded logic/signal traces: `decode_signal_recording` with explicit decoder,
  channel and protocol settings. On Linux with util-linux prlimit, supply sigrok-cli 0.7.2 through
  `REA_SIGROK_COMMAND`; see [recording guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/signal-recordings.md).
  Output defaults to 50 literal lines; select annotation classes and page with
  `line_offset` / `line_limit`, or explicit null for all remaining output.
  Window counts are display lines, not annotations or samples. Preserve source digests across pages.
  This reads existing files; it does not acquire hardware signals.
- Explicit local WebAssembly artifact: `inspect_wasm_artifact`. Supply WABT 1.0.42
  through `REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY`; retain exact byte/tool identity and decoded WAT.
  Select JavaScript glue and candidate paths explicitly and preserve URL/path
  ambiguity. No implicit fetch or target execution; WAT is not original source.
  See the [WASM guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/wasm-artifacts.md).
- Explicit local EVM bytecode carrier: `inspect_evm_interface` with caller-selected
  `raw` or `hex` encoding. Preserve carrier/decoded digests and treat selectors,
  argument strings and mutability as inferred candidates; this performs no chain
  lookup or target execution. For the complete inferred interface without hex or
  duplicate stdout, discover support and select `detail: "summary"`; complete
  Evidence stays retained under its original identity. Use the returned
  `parent_evidence_id` for exact function or `bytecode_hex`/stdout/stderr pages.
  Candidate coverage does not establish interface completeness. See the
  [EVM bytecode guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/evm-bytecode.md).
- Embedded Go compiler, module or build-setting metadata: `inspect_go_binary`
  with the explicit local file. This built-in target-free inspection requires no
  Go installation or disassembler. Preserve raw module bytes and source ranges;
  absent metadata does not prove a binary is not Go, and unparsed text records
  remain explicit. See the
  [Go binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/go-binaries.md).
- Embedded cargo-auditable Rust dependency metadata: `inspect_rust_binary`
  with the explicit local ELF, PE, or thin Mach-O file. This built-in
  target-free inspection requires no Rust installation or disassembler. Preserve
  package order, dependency indices, and the section file range. A missing
  `.dep-v0` section is null metadata, not proof the binary has no dependencies.
  A rustc commit hash is an inference from a read-only `/rustc/<40-hex>/` path.
  See the
  [Rust binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/rust-binaries.md).

- Explicit local SQLite database snapshot: `inspect_sqlite_database`. Inspect
  with Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ providing native SQLite limits. Read schema
  first (compact inventory by default), or select an exact ordinary table
  and `columns` when rows are needed. Defaults are selected-table schema and
  20 rows; request `schema_scope: "database"` for the complete stored schema. Preserve both database and existing sibling WAL identity; row samples
  report truncation and have unspecified order. Use a quiescent snapshot rather
  than assuming a live database/WAL pair was copied atomically. See the
  [SQLite guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/sqlite-databases.md).
- Explicit Linux ELF file for offline layout, symbols, relocations or static
  mitigation evidence: `inspect_binary_layout`. This target-free operation uses
  caller-supplied pwntools without opening a disassembler database. Preserve its
  raw locations and inference/coverage limits; see the
  [offline binary guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/binary-diagnostics.md).
- Supplied Linux x86-64 ELF core: `inspect_recorded_crash`. Read every recorded
  thread, raw note and source-bound register without opening a live target.
  Historical PIDs do not select live processes. Request `include_debugger_context`
  only when core-only mapping candidates help; see the
  [recorded crash guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/recorded-crashes.md).
- PE resource type/name/language trees and static icon group references:
  `inspect_pe_resources` with an explicit path. This portable operation requires
  no active target or engine; opaque payloads retain file ranges and SHA-256.
- Native executable, library, or analysis database: `open_binary`, then
  use focused analysis tools directly; call `binary_overview` when metadata or
  inventory context is useful and available from the selected provider.

For an existing IDA MCP configuration, use `open_binary` with the original
input binary and `provider_id: "ida"`; do not pass an `.idb` or `.i64` database.
The legacy attached profile binds the already-open GUI input by SHA-256 and
leaves its database open. The modern headless profile creates and closes an
owned private database without saving. Installation and registration reuse
[mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp](https://github.com/mrexodia/ida-pro-mcp); see the
[IDA provider guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/ida-provider.md).
Proceed directly to `analyze_function`, pseudocode, or function/string searches
after opening; IDA does not supply `binary_overview`. Consult session availability
when composing broader workflows. Modern direct callers and unsupported dossier
facets remain unknown; live IDA results are not replayed from snapshots.

With `REA_KUNA_COMMAND` configured, `provider_id: "kuna"` answers procedure
lists, lookups, pseudocode, assembly and `analyze_function` from Kuna's cached
whole-program export. Callers/callees use a separate body-free graph shared by
the session; `xrefs` returns exact-address incoming sites and filters forwarding
aliases. These queries and inventory lookups do not trigger a C export. Indirect
targets remain unknown and can make relationship coverage partial. Reference
caches expire on close; a fresh CLI process repeats the native reference walk.
Typed references, CFG, raw-memory tools and annotations remain unsupported. A cold first
answer can come from a single-function run (its limitations say so); assembly
waits for the export. For pseudocode and assembly, `raw_result.source` names the
cached `.c`/`.asm` file and byte span, which you may search directly instead of
calling per function. See the
[Kuna provider guide](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/main/docs/kuna-provider.md).

If the user says only "my app" without a name, path, or target already selected
for this task, ask which app before searching for artifacts. Paths in unrelated
saved reports and nearby test fixtures do not select the user's target. Resolve
an actual human-readable app name to one clear installed artifact when possible;
ask when matches are ambiguous. Never choose an example app on the user's behalf.

In a target-free session, use `open_binary` to bind any archive/package or
native target whose analysis tool operates on the active target. Do not call an
unadvertised tool; inspect `binary_session` with `{}` and its
`result.tool_availability` for availability reasons and remediation. Expand each
group's `names` into entries, inheriting the inventory-level client requirements
unless the group overrides them. In its closed effect and annotation vocabularies,
listed flags are true and omitted known flags are false. The grouped name union
is the complete tool inventory; use `tools/list` for canonical tool schemas.
Provider candidate facts describe possible providers, while top-level session
capabilities describe the current route and `analysis_provider_binding` names the
selected provider. Do not treat those scopes as interchangeable.

## Work summary-first

Start with the default result and use its inline Evidence and graph context.
For a JavaScript application or ELF layout whose size is unknown or large,
call `analyze_javascript_application` or `inspect_binary_layout` with
`"detail": "summary"`, then inspect the retained `parent_evidence_id` with
`inspect_analysis_view`.
Page module identities and select the returned `node_id` before requesting an
item; a single file path can represent several graph roles. Do not repeat an
identical analysis or rejected call without a changed input or resolved blocker.
Recheck session state when a lifecycle change makes that status useful.
Make a focused follow-up only when the
returned result leaves a specific question unanswered.

If MCP reports `resource_constraint` with `details.resource: "transport"`, call
`inspect_analysis_view` with its reported same-session Evidence reference for a
summary, one section/module, or a stable page. Use `trace_application_feature`
once a seed is known, or call `export_evidence_bundle` to write the complete
session to a selected path. The analysis remains complete in the ledger; avoid
repeating it merely to request the same oversized response. Complete CLI JSON
output also streams without a single MCP frame.

When the retained parent ID is unknown, use `get_evidence_bundle` with
`detail: "summary"` and exact filters for operation, target SHA-256,
analysis-profile digest or canonical procedure address. Select its returned
Evidence ID for the next view instead of requesting the complete bundle.
`retention: "complete-record"` means the whole record is stored; native
value-flow truncation and unknown metadata remain separate. For an exported
portable bundle, use `rea inspect-evidence-bundle` with JSON containing `path`,
`detail: "summary"` and the same `filters`. Reading that file still requires
validating its full contents within the local memory budget.

A client can also truncate a successful tool result without a REA transport
error. Treat that preview as incomplete; use the retained parent ID for smaller
views or export when the full record is needed. Do not parse the preview as
canonical JSON or repeat the producer. For JavaScript, read the
[module-view and trace recipes](references/javascript-applications.md) before
drilling into a large graph; a broad bidirectional trace can expand unrelated
containment relationships even after summary analysis.

Every conclusion must distinguish observations, inferences, and unknowns. Cite
Evidence IDs, preserve limitations and incomplete coverage, and never imply
that static analysis observed execution. Runtime requests execute the declared
target and lifecycle; do not broaden the target or action beyond those fields.

Within the user's requested investigation, call available analysis tools
directly. REA does not require permission grants or per-call approval flags.
The agent client can independently require approval. Follow the declared request
scope and the host's actual access requirements; use the recovery guide for an
observed client-policy rejection.

## Plan broader investigations

For requests that span multiple features or subsystems, use a staged workflow:

1. Turn the request into a checklist of questions and the evidence each answer
   needs. Resolve target identity and constraints from the conversation and
   workspace before asking for information again.
2. Inspect the current REA session, artifact identity, saved analysis database,
   bookmarks, and prior evidence. Reuse matching state; do not open duplicate
   sessions or repeat identical analysis.
3. Start with the smallest useful overview or inventory. Follow each question
   from its entry point through relevant data and state changes to its result.
   Batch related operations around a specific hypothesis, then expand only when
   the returned evidence leaves a concrete gap.
4. Inspect relevant packaged resources and configuration alongside code when
   they affect the question. Use format-aware inventory and parsers; do not
   infer behavior from filenames, strings, or layout alone.
5. Corroborate a conclusion with the evidence type it requires. Use runtime
   observation only when static evidence cannot answer the question and the
   required host runtime and OS access are available. For JavaScript behavior,
   run probes against the actual app through the available browser, Electron,
   or process capture workflow.
6. Decompose work into independent questions. When parallel workers are
   available and the questions do not depend on one another, assign distinct
   scopes, point workers to existing evidence, and ask them to return sources,
   conclusions, and unresolved gaps. Otherwise, work sequentially.
7. Keep a concise finding ledger linking each conclusion to Evidence IDs,
   confidence/evidence type, search boundary, and remaining unknowns. Update
   the shared index or investigation report so later passes can reuse results.

Before finishing, revisit the original checklist. Mark each question as
answered, partially answered, or unresolved based on its evidence; keep
bounded negative searches bounded, and do not describe a broad investigation
as complete while required questions remain open.

## Finish the task

Explain findings in plain language and tie them to returned evidence. When the
user asks to build something, use normal coding tools and separate observed
behavior from design choices. Close an opened native session with
`close_binary` when the investigation is complete.
